hints: Look closely at the symmetry of the starting ketone, pentan-3-one, and what groups will be attached to the carbonyl carbon after addition.
Draw the product as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and check if the central carbon really has four different groups.
Recall how $\text{HCN}$ adds to a $\text{C=O}$ bond, which species actually attacks first and what is regenerated at the end.
walkthrough:
**Identify the carbonyl compound**

This is pentan-3-one, a symmetrical ketone. The carbonyl carbon is joined to two identical ethyl groups.

Starting material:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$$

**Draw the cyanohydrin product**

Addition of HCN across C=O gives both an OH and a CN on the same carbon.

Product:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$
The central carbon has two $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ groups, plus OH and CN. Because two groups are identical, it is not chiral.

**Recall the correct mechanism type**

The carbonyl carbon is electron poor (delta positive), so it is attacked by a nucleophile, not an electrophile. The nucleophile is the cyanide ion, $\text{CN}^-$.

First step:
$$\text{C=O} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{C(CN)-O}^-$$
This intermediate is an alkoxide ion with $\text{C-O}^-$, not $\text{C-OH}$ yet. Protonation comes later.

**See why cyanide is a catalyst**

Pure HCN is a weak acid and provides very little $\text{CN}^-$. A small amount of $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ is added to supply $\text{CN}^-$.

Second step regenerates it:
$$\text{C(CN)-O}^- + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{C(CN)-OH} + \text{CN}^-$$
Since $\text{CN}^-$ is reformed, it acts as a catalyst.

options.A: Incorrect. A chiral centre needs four different groups. Here the product carbon is bonded to two identical $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ groups, plus OH and CN, so it is achiral. Students often assume all cyanohydrins from ketones are chiral, but symmetry here prevents it.
options.B: Incorrect. Addition to aldehydes and ketones with HCN is nucleophilic addition. The $\text{CN}^-$ ion donates a pair of electrons to the delta positive carbonyl carbon. Electrophilic addition is typical of alkenes with bromine or HBr, not carbonyls.
options.C: Incorrect. The first intermediate after $\text{CN}^-$ attack is a negatively charged alkoxide, $\text{C(CN)-O}^-$. The $\text{O-H}$ bond only forms in the second step when this ion takes $\text{H}^+$ from HCN. So no C-OH is present in the intermediate.
options.D: Correct. HCN alone reacts very slowly because it is weakly dissociated. Added cyanide ions from KCN or NaCN provide the strong nucleophile $\text{CN}^-$ to start the attack, and $\text{CN}^-$ is regenerated when the alkoxide is protonated, so it is a catalyst.
